newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia says will resist US stand on labour at WTO.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says will resist US stand on labour at WTO.

text.p: Malaysia said on Monday it is standing firm on its position that labour standards, rules on government procurement and investments should not be on the agenda of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

"If the U.S. stands firm and would not back away from its position on government procurement and labour standards, this would mean that these issues would not make their way into the declaration at all," Malaysia's international trade and industry minister Rafidah Aziz told reporters.
"And for Malaysia, that will be the best thing that could happen."
Asked to respond to Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky's statement earlier on Monday linking trade and human rights, Rafidah said:

"No, we don't agree. You don't link trade to human rights. You don't link trade action to labour standards and other social clauses. That is the stand of Malaysia and I am happy to say with many other countries too."

Barshefsky told the WTO delegates: "We believe strongly that increased trade and economic growth that it brings should also engender greater respect for the basic human rights which are the focus of our core labour standards proposal."
Rafidah said Malaysia's stand was shared by its partners in ASEAN (the Association of South East Asian Nations) -- Thailand, Indonesia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore and Vietnam.
She said Malaysia was against investment rules on the WTO's agenda "because we have our own domestic equity condition...and that goes for many countries."
Labour standards should not even be included in the WTO work programme as this is best left to the International Labour Organisation, she said.

Rafidah said Malaysia has forwarded an amendment to the U.S. text on rules pertaining to government procurement. In its proposal, Malaysia agreed to form a group to examine and develop a multilateral agreement to encourage transparency in the process of government procurement.
"We said that in bringing about discipline in procurement in the future, we need to take into account the national policies of WTO members."
Rafidah said Malaysia would chair a Tuesday meeting of 15 developing countries to discuss agriculture, textile, government procurement, investment rules, labour standards and policy on competition.
